To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
The language of poverty is a discourse of power and control.

(a) there is an over-representation of the poor in the news media; (b) the media tend to portray the poor in stereotypical ways; and (c) the media tend not to portray the poor as agents of their own lives.

(i) the discourse on poverty in the British press is dominated by the language of the individual, (ii) the discourse on welfare reform is dominated by the discourse of blame, (iii) the discourse on workfare is dominated by the discourses of the individual and of blame, and (iv) the discourse of the individual and the discourse of blame are closely related
In summary, our research is concerned with
the analysis of poverty discourse in the media.
how language is used to create and reinforce ideologies and how these ideologies can be challenged.
how language is used to construct and maintain social inequality.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the use of corpus linguistics and critical discourse analysis in poverty research is beneficial in terms of providing a deeper understanding of poverty and its causes, effects, and consequences.
the corpus linguistic approach to CDA is a powerful tool for the analysis of discourse and the social phenomena that it is used to describe.
the combination of CDA and corpus linguistics is a powerful and effective methodological approach for the investigation of language use in social and political contexts.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we are interested in the way in which poverty is represented in the media, and how this representation may influence people’s attitudes to and perceptions of poverty.
we have combined corpus linguistics and critical discourse analysis to explore how the discourse of poverty in the UK has been constructed and maintained in the media over the last 30 years.
it combines the quantitative approach of corpus linguistics with the qualitative approach of critical discourse analysis.
The main takeaway from our work is that
corpus analysis can help us identify patterns of language use that we would not have otherwise noticed, and can help us to see how these patterns are used in the service of social inequality.

corpus linguistics and critical discourse analysis can be used in combination to reveal how language can be used to construct and reinforce social inequality and how this inequality can be contested and challenged.
corpus analysis can help to provide a more nuanced picture of the way in which poverty is represented.
